analysis.one_liner: Lets small businesses and self-employed people band together to buy group health plans under relaxed rules.
analysis.headline: Backed by 6 Republican senators, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law the criteria of a 2018 Labor Department rule that let small businesses, trade groups, and self-employed "working owners" join together to sponsor a single group health plan — a power a federal judge had stripped away in 2019. Plans formed this way are governed by large-employer rules, which don't impose every requirement that applies to small-group and individual plans, though the bill bars plans from discriminating based on health status. It also gives statutory footing to short-term, limited-duration insurance plans that last under a year, which under current law are exempt from rules like coverage of preexisting conditions. The bill went nowhere: it sat in the Senate health committee until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners, their employees, self-employed people, and members of trade or professional associations who could pool together to buy coverage with more bargaining power and, in some cases, fewer required benefits and lower premiums. Health insurers and associations would also gain a new market to sell into.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets groups of small employers band together and sponsor a group health plan as if they were a single large employer, giving them the combined bargaining power the bill's findings say produced average premium decreases of up to 29% for small businesses in some cases.
Association plans formed under the bill cannot deny membership or charge different premiums based on a person's health status, medical history, or claims experience.

Self-employed people who work at least 20 hours a week or earn enough in self-employment income could qualify as both employer and employee, letting them join an association plan even without other employees.

The bill would restore, by statute, the framework of a 2018 Labor Department rule that a federal district judge vacated in March 2019, which the bill's findings say threatened coverage for existing enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: If healthier people and small firms move into cheaper association or short-term plans, the people left behind in the regular individual and small-group markets — disproportionately older or sicker people — could face higher premiums as risk pools shrink. People who bought a skimpier plan and later got sick could find it covers less than an ACA-compliant plan would.
analysis.who_pays_short: People remaining in regular insurance risk pools

drawbacks.text: Cheaper plans can mean fewer covered services: short-term, limited-duration plans are currently exempt from Affordable Care Act market rules including preexisting-condition protections, and the bill would give those plans statutory standing while allowing coverage periods of under 12 months.

When healthier enrollees shift into association or short-term plans, the individual and small-group markets are left with a smaller, sicker pool, which pushes premiums up for everyone who stays — the core criticism of association plan expansions when pursued by regulation.

Association plans have a history of financial failure leaving members with unpaid medical bills; the bill relies on state oversight of self-insured arrangements for that risk, as its own findings acknowledge, and confirms that joining a plan creates no employer or joint-employer relationship under federal or state law — a protection written for franchisors and their franchisees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a healthy self-employed person or small firm facing high premiums, pooling with others could genuinely cut costs, and the bill's nondiscrimination rules are real protections. But the savings partly come from splitting risk pools and offering plans that don't have to meet every standard that applies to regular coverage, so the gains to one group come partly at the expense of people left in the traditional market. The joint-employer shield for franchisors also serves business interests beyond health coverage. It is a real trade-off, not a clean win, and it never received a hearing where these questions could be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill on March 23, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Five Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no further activity: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing insurance market structure stayed exactly as it was: insurers selling ACA-compliant plans kept their customer base intact, and people with preexisting conditions faced no new competition from skimpier plans. Small businesses and self-employed people who wanted the pooling option got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent insurers and the ACA market

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Association Health Plans Act of 2021 in the Senate.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans — Sen. Kennedy plus 5 of the Senate's 50 Republicans — with no Democratic support on the record, and the bill died without action in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill creates a new market: insurers could sell association plans to small-employer groups under large-group rules, which don't require every coverage standard that applies to individual and small-group plans. Insurers profit either way, but cheaper skimpier plans can pull healthier customers out of the regular market, raising costs for everyone left in it.

The bill says joining or facilitating an association plan creates no employer or joint-employer relationship under any federal or state law, written to cover franchisors and franchisees. That shields franchise companies from joint-employer liability, which matters to franchise workers seeking to hold the parent company accountable.

Associations of employers gain the power to sponsor health coverage for their members as a single large employer, a service they could offer alongside their existing work. Their interest in cheaper member coverage runs alongside small businesses' interests.

The bill gives these plans statutory authority to cover periods of under 12 months; under current law they are exempt from ACA market rules including preexisting-condition protections, so their business model is selling cheaper coverage to healthy people.
